content: Endometrial cancer, which is cancer of the uterine lining, is the fifth most common cancer among women globally and the fourth most common in high-income countries, where its incidence is rising. Each year, approximately 319,605 new cases of endometrial cancer are diagnosed worldwide, with 9,000 cases in the UK and 61,380 in the USA. Endometrial hyperplasia refers to an overgrowth of the uterine lining and can act as a precursor to certain types of endometrial cancer. It is classified as a proliferative endometrial lesion. The incidence of endometrial hyperplasia is 133 per 100,000 women annually, while atypical endometrial hyperplasia occurs at a rate of 54 per 100,000 women per year. The 2014 World Health Organization (WHO) classification of endometrial hyperplasia includes two categories: hyperplasia without atypia and atypical hyperplasia/endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia. This simplified classification reflects new findings on molecular genetic changes. Hyperplasia without atypia typically regresses and lacks significant genetic changes, whereas atypical endometrial hyperplasia shares many genetic mutations with endometrioid endometrial cancer, such as microsatellite instability, PAX2 inactivation, PTEN mutations, KRAS mutations, and CTNNB1 (β-catenin) mutations. Atypical hyperplasia has a high co-incidence or progression rate to endometrial cancer. The progression rates to cancer differ between hyperplasia with and without atypia. Hyperplasia without atypia progresses to cancer in 1% to 5% of cases, while atypical hyperplasia progresses in 8% to 27% of cases. However, this may be underestimated, as co-existing carcinoma has been reported in 36% to 59% of women undergoing hysterectomy for atypical hyperplasia. Endometrial cancer is most common in postmenopausal women, but 15% to 25% of cases are diagnosed in premenopausal women. Four percent of cases occur in women under 40 years old, and 7% to 10% occur in women under 45 years old. The most common type of endometrial cancer is endometrioid adenocarcinoma, which is often diagnosed at an early stage and has a favorable prognosis. In young women, fiveand ten-year disease-free survival rates after standard surgical treatment (hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy) are 99.2% and 98%, respectively. It is commonly believed that young women with endometrial cancer are more likely to have early-stage, low-risk tumors. However, population-based data indicate that only 18% of women younger than 45 years have stage IA grade 1 endometrial cancer. Obesity is a major risk factor for endometrial hyperplasia and endometrioid endometrial adenocarcinoma. Obesity is associated with the peripheral conversion of androgens to estrogens by adipose tissue. Other risk factors include a sedentary lifestyle, hyperinsulinemia, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, hypertension, nulliparity, early menarche, and anovulation. Many of these factors are related to obesity. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), the most common endocrine disorder associated with anovulation, is also a common cause of infertility. In women with PCOS, increased peripheral conversion of estrogens and the lack of progesterone release due to anovulation may contribute to the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer. Progesterone, produced during ovulatory cycles by the ovarian corpus luteum, plays a critical role in counteracting the proliferative effects of estrogens on the endometrium. Nulliparity itself is a risk factor for endometrial cancer, as nulliparous women miss periods of high progesterone levels during pregnancy. Young nulliparous women with endometrial carcinoma may be interested in fertility-sparing treatment. These women should be informed that standard surgical treatment for endometrial cancer or atypical hyperplasia has excellent survival outcomes but precludes fertility. Unfortunately, many of these women may have underlying subfertility, so even without a diagnosis of atypical hyperplasia or endometrial cancer, their chances of becoming pregnant may be low. Fertility after conservative treatment for atypical hyperplasia and endometrial cancer depends on the response to cancer treatment and underlying factors affecting fertility, such as the presence of PCOS. Discussions about the appropriateness of fertility-sparing surgery should balance potential risks with realistic expectations about achieving pregnancy on an individual basis. Ovulation induction treatment may be necessary, but it may increase the risk of atypical hyperplasia and cancer. Progesterone treatment for endometrial atypical hyperplasia and cancer has shown live birth rates between 25% and 35%, with higher rates achieved using assisted reproductive techniques. Progestin treatment may also be considered for older, postmenopausal women at very high surgical risk, although this represents a different clinical scenario. The 2018 National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend fertility-sparing management for well-differentiated (grade 1) endometrioid endometrial carcinoma limited to the endometrium, as determined by imaging (MRI or ultrasound). There should be no contraindications to medical therapy or pregnancy. Other scientific societies provide similar recommendations for selecting candidates for fertility-sparing management. Medical management of endometrioid endometrial cancer or atypical hyperplasia has been based on progestogens, administered orally or via a levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (IUS). Some studies have shown the efficacy of metformin in proliferative disorders of the endometrium, including atypical hyperplasia and early-stage endometrial cancer. Other hormone treatments targeting estrogen levels include gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonists and aromatase inhibitors. Weight loss interventions, including lifestyle changes and bariatric surgery, may improve survival in women with endometrial cancer or atypical hyperplasia by addressing obesity-related pathways. Bariatric surgery has been shown to reduce glucose, insulin, and IGF-1 levels and improve insulin sensitivity in obese women. However, there is limited high-quality evidence on the effectiveness of weight loss as a treatment for endometrial cancer or atypical hyperplasia. Progesterone is recommended as the first-line treatment for women with endometrial cancer or atypical hyperplasia who wish to preserve fertility. However, data on the optimal drug, route of administration, dose, and duration of treatment remain unclear. Other treatments, such as metformin or bariatric surgery, are being investigated and may play a role in conservative management. Women considering fertility-preserving treatment should understand the limitations and risks of these therapies to make informed decisions.
